item.title: Measles outbreak: Death toll reaches 960 as five more die in 24 hours
item.description:
Five children died with measles-like symptoms in the 24 hours until 8:00am on Friday, bringing the country’s combined tally of confirmed and suspected measles-related deaths to 960 this year.
The Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) has classified all five latest fatalities as suspected measles deaths.
With these, the total number of suspected measles deaths has reached 861, while confirmed deaths from measles have remained the same at 99.
A total of 1,100 new suspected measles cases were reported during the 24-hour period, bringing the cumulative number of suspected cases nationwide to 154,792.
Meanwhile, 70 new confirmed measles cases were recorded, bringing the total number of laboratory-confirmed infections to 18,796.
Since March 15 this year, a total of 135,473 patients with suspected measles have been hospitalised across the country, of whom 130,457 have recovered, according to DGHS data.

Bangladesh confirms deal to buy Chinese J-10 fighter jets: report
item.description:
Bangladesh has confirmed a deal to purchase China’s 4.5-generation J-10CE fighter jets, citing the aircraft’s reported combat performance against French-made Rafale jets during the brief Pakistan-India conflict in May, the South China Morning Post (SCMP) reported on Friday.

The Chengdu J-10C is a single-engine, multirole combat aircraft manufactured in China. Boasting a top speed of Mach 1.8, it can be fitted with a variety of air-to-air and air-to-ground munitions. It played a key role on the first night of hostilities, shooting down six jets belonging to the Indian Air Force.

The Information and Broadcasting Adviser to the Prime Minister of Bangladesh Zahedur Rahman said earlier this week that a draft proposal to buy the jets had been submitted to the country’s finance ministry and Armed Forces Division for final approval, SCMP reported citing the Bangladeshi Press Information Department (PID).

According to the Bangladesh PID, the draft proposal also includes the purchase of Chinese attack helicopters, VIP transport helicopters and drones.

“Subject to necessary budgetary allocation in the current fiscal year, this procurement will be executed immediately; otherwise, it will roll over into the next budget cycle,” it added.

SCMP reports that Rahman said Bangladesh “paid attention” to the war last year, when Pakistan used J-10 fighters and PL-15 long-range air-to-air missiles to shoot down Indian Rafales.

In January this year, Pakistan and Bangladesh’s air chiefs held detailed discussions on the “potential procurement” of the locally-produced JF-17 Thunder aircraft, according to Inter-Services Public Relations.

It added that Bangladesh Air Force Air Chief Marshal Hasan Mahmood Khan called on Pakistan Air Force Air Chief Marshal Zaheer Ahmed Babar Sidhu in Islamabad, where “The meeting focused on strengthening operational cooperation and institutional synergy, with emphasis on training, capacity building, and collaboration in aerospace advancements.”

A day later, Dhaka’s air chief discussed avenues for enhancing defence cooperation with Pakistan in separate meetings with Chief of Defence Forces (CDF) and Chief of the Army Staff (COAS) Field Marshal Asim Munir, and Chief of the Naval Staff Admiral Naveed Ashraf.

A year ago, Pakistan was engaged in a military conflict with India, dealing the boastful neighbour an internationally recognised “clear setback”.

The conflict with India, starting from the April 22 Pahalgam attack to the end of Operation Bunyanum Marsoos, with a ceasefire ending a military escalation between the two countries on May 10, has been called “Marka-i-Haq” (Battle of Truth) by the state.

But from the night of May 6 to May 10, the drums of war were echoing loudly across South Asia as the nuclear-armed arch-rivals exchanged missiles, raising global alarm over the risk of unpredictable escalation.

Human Rights Commission Bill: Opposition MPs skip parliamentary committee discussion
item.description:
Opposition members of parliament (MPs) did not participate in discussions on the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) Bill at the Parliamentary Standing Committee on the Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs.

They have decided to refrain from participating at any stage of the bill’s passage. Their reasons have been set out in writing and submitted to the parliamentary committee.

After the bill was introduced in the Jatiya Sangsad (national parliament) on Thursday, it was referred to the Parliamentary Standing Committee on the Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs for scrutiny and submission of a report.

The committee met at the Jatiya Sangsad Bhaban on Sunday morning. The meeting was scheduled to discuss the Property Transfer Bill and the National Human Rights Commission Bill.

While the opposition MPs took part in the discussion on the Property Transfer Bill, they did not participate in the discussion on the NHRC bill. Instead, they left the meeting.

Nazibur Rahman, a member of the Parliamentary Standing Committee on the Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs and a Jamaat-e-Islami MP, confirmed the matter to journalists.

The opposition has three MPs on the parliamentary standing committee: Nazibur Rahman, Al Faruk Abdul Latif and Akhtar Hossain. The three MPs have submitted a written statement to the committee setting out their position, a copy of which was also provided to journalists.

The written statement says the government repealed the National Human Rights Commission Ordinance 2025 unilaterally, disregarding the views of victims, stakeholders and national and international human rights organisations. At the time of the repeal, the government had pledged to enact stronger and more effective legislation. Instead, the statement says, a bill that is weaker and narrower in scope has been placed before Parliament.

It further states that the proposed bill is not consistent with the internationally recognised standards of the global alliance of national human rights institutions, the Paris Principles, or relevant international conventions and declarations. The committee was instructed to submit its report within just two working days, which, according to the opposition MPs, has effectively curtailed the opportunity for proper consultation with stakeholders and for the bill to be independently scrutinised and assessed.

This, they said, has created a situation in which the standing committee risks being reduced to a “rubber stamp”.

In their letter, the three MPs said that, for these reasons, the opposition members of the Parliamentary Standing Committee on the Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs had decided not to participate in any discussion or scrutiny of the bill and to refrain from taking part at any stage of the process for its passage.

They also decided not to attend meetings of the standing committee.

Appellate Division: Writ not maintainable where contract provides for arbitration
item.description:
The Appellate Division of the Supreme Court has held that where a contract provides for arbitration, mediation or another alternative mechanism to resolve disputes arising after its execution, a party cannot bypass that mechanism and directly file a writ petition with the High Court.
The observation came in a judgment published on the Supreme Court website on Sunday.
The Appellate Division made the observation while dismissing a civil appeal challenging an earlier judgment concerning the execution of a contract through negotiation or settlement.
The court said that where a contract provides an effective alternative remedy for resolving a dispute, there is no scope for directly invoking the High Court's writ jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution.
The judgment was delivered in the case of M/s AMS Faraz Construction vs State.
The full 37-page judgment, delivered on February 22 by a five-member bench headed by Chief Justice Zubayer Rahman Chowdhury, was published on August 25.
The judgment said that even when a statutory authority is a party to a contract involving the sale of government assets, a party that has violated the terms of the contract cannot seek redress by filing a writ petition. Where the contract contains an effective arbitration clause or provides another alternative mechanism for dispute resolution, the party must pursue that remedy before seeking relief under Article 102.
According to the case documents, Chisty Textile Mills was established in 1966 on about 16 acres of land in Daulatpur of Adarsha Sadar upazila in Comilla. The mill was nationalized in 1972.
Production at the factory was later suspended and its workers were dismissed under a golden handshake scheme. Bangladesh Textile Mills Corporation (BTMC) subsequently resumed operations, but the mill was eventually closed amid continued losses. On November 9, 2003, the government decided to liquidate it.
After a liquidator was appointed to sell the state-owned mill, Md Faruk Islam Bhuiyan, proprietor of AMS Faraz Construction Ltd of Ganganagar in Kasba upazila, Brahmanbaria, expressed interest in purchasing it.
The Ministry of Textiles and Jute subsequently valued the mill at Tk35 crore and signed an agreement with Faraz Construction on January 1, 2014. Under the agreement, the company was required to pay Tk15 crore as a down payment and the remaining Tk20 crore in five equal instalments.
The government handed over the mill and its land to Faraz Construction on January 9, 2014.
However, allegations later surfaced that the factory had been sold without a tender or open auction and at a price significantly below its actual value.
Several national dailies reported on February 11, 2014, alleging irregularities in the liquidation process and claiming that property worth Tk350 crore had been sold for Tk35 crore.
The government subsequently issued an order directing Faruk Islam Bhuiyan to refrain from carrying out activities related to the mill and stopped accepting the outstanding instalments. Faraz Construction had already defaulted on the second instalment.
Faraz Construction later sought withdrawal of the order, but the government rejected its request. Following instructions from the Prime Minister's Office, BTMC issued an order on April 17, 2014, suspending all activities at the mill until further instructions.
Faraz Construction subsequently sought withdrawal of the suspension order. After receiving a response, the company served a legal notice and later filed a writ petition with the High Court in 2014 after receiving no further response.
The High Court issued a rule and, after hearing both sides, disposed of it on June 15, 2015, with several directions.
The High Court directed the authorities to allow Faraz Construction to resume operations at Chisty Textile Mills and to accept the remaining instalments. It also directed the execution and registration of the necessary sale deed in favour of Faraz Construction in accordance with the law and the terms of the January 1, 2014 agreement with BTMC.
The government subsequently appealed against the High Court judgment. On July 3, 2018, the Appellate Division set aside the High Court judgment and order.
Faraz Construction filed a civil review petition against the Appellate Division judgment in 2019. The petition was accepted for hearing on March 6, 2025. On February 22, 2026, the five-member Appellate Division bench dismissed the review petition.
In its judgment, the Appellate Division said the liquidator had no authority under the agreement to sell the mill through any process other than a tender or open auction.
Therefore, once the agreement was executed, the mill could not be transferred without following the procedure prescribed in the agreement. The court also observed that the process followed for transferring the mill did not comply with the law.
The court said the appellants themselves had violated important terms and conditions of the agreement and therefore could not seek legal remedy through a writ petition based on the alleged agreement.
The judgment further said that when parties to a contract choose arbitration as the forum for resolving disputes arising from the agreement, a party cannot bypass that mechanism and seek direct enforcement of the contract under Article 102 of the Constitution.
“In this context, this division is of the opinion that where a dispute arises out of an obligation to comply with a contract and the contract itself provides for settlement of the dispute through arbitration or any other forum, the aggrieved party should pursue the remedy prescribed in the contract without invoking the exceptional jurisdiction of the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution,” the judgment said.
The court also noted that Faraz Construction had failed to comply with the payment schedule under the contract and had not pursued the arbitration mechanism provided in the agreement.
Finding no manifest error in the judgment under review, the Appellate Division dismissed the civil appeal.

item.title: Delhi denies permission for seminar featuring speakers linked to Awami League
item.description:
Permission was denied for an international seminar in Delhi because it was due to feature speakers linked to the Awami League. The Delhi Police refused to grant clearance, telling the organisers that the event could not be permitted because of “certain controversies”.

The seminar was scheduled to take place yesterday, Saturday, from 6:00 pm to 8.30 pm. The organisers had also requested the Delhi Police to make the necessary security arrangements to ensure that the event could proceed without disruption.

The event was organised by the Foreign Correspondents Club of South Asia (FCC) in New Delhi. Its theme was “Europe and Asia: From Dialogue to a Partnership”. The FCC organised the seminar jointly with the Belgium-based organisation Hand in Hand Foundation.

Although no official explanation has been issued for the cancellation, it is believed that the Delhi Police withheld permission because some of the participants were linked to the Awami League, whose activities are banned in Bangladesh.

Tensions in relations between the two countries had emerged following a virtual appearance by Bangladesh’s ousted former prime minister Sheikh Hasina at the same club on 5 August, during which she commented on the situation in Bangladesh.

The Bangladesh government not only formally protested the incident but also sought assurances that such “undesirable provocations” would not be allowed to recur.

Following this, Dhaka also renewed and intensified its demand for Hasina’s extradition. Subsequently, a possible visit to India by Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman was postponed.

Well-informed quarters believe Saturday’s seminar was denied permission, possibly to prevent any fresh controversy from emerging.

They regard the decision as evidence of India’s sincerity in improving relations with the Bangladesh government. India’s Ministry of External Affairs has said on several occasions, in connection with the controversy surrounding Hasina, that the government had nothing to do with what was said from that platform and that the remarks did not represent the position of the Indian government.

According to diplomatic sources familiar with the matter, by stopping Saturday’s seminar, Delhi also sought to convey to Bangladesh that, in the interests of bilateral relations, India no longer wants any unnecessary controversy.

Selim Mahmud, the Awami League’s information and research secretary, was due to attend Saturday’s seminar at the FCC. The party’s activities are currently banned in Bangladesh. Also invited was Nurun Nabi, a freedom fighter and Bangladeshi-American scientist.

Other invited speakers included former Indian High Commissioner to Bangladesh Veena Sikri; Rohingya rights activist Ravi Alam; United Diplomatic Council President Asif Iqbal; and Hand in Hand Foundation General Secretary Golam Jilani, among others.

Czech politician Ondřej Dostál and German politician Peter Fahrenholz were also expected to attend the seminar.

Part of the event was to be devoted to a question-and-answer session. It is believed that the Delhi Police did not want the situation in Bangladesh to become the subject of adverse or contentious remarks during the session.

The Delhi Police informed the organisers on Saturday that permission for the event could not be granted. The application was annotated by hand, citing “certain controversies” as the reason for refusing permission.

FCC President Wael Awwad told the media that the event had been intended to focus on partnership and development. “It was an intellectual discussion. I am not sure why the Delhi Police denied permission,” he said.

item.title: New pay scale for govt employees may go before cabinet Monday
item.description:
A draft of the new pay structure for government officials and employees has been prepared, and it may be placed before the Cabinet for approval tomorrow, Monday, sources at the Ministry of Finance told Prothom Alo.

If approved, the process of issuing the official gazette notification will begin, which could take one to two weeks, the sources added.

A 10-member committee, headed by Cabinet Secretary Nasimul Ghani, was formed on 21 April to recommend the implementation of a new pay structure for government employees. The committee has now finalised its recommendations.

Nearly 12 years after the 8th Pay Commission, the interim government formed the 23-member 9th National Pay Commission on 27 July 2025. The commission, headed by former Finance Secretary Zakir Ahmed Khan, submitted its report to then Chief Adviser Professor Muhammad Yunus on 21 January this year.

While retaining the existing 20-grade structure, the Zakir Ahmed Khan commission recommended increases of between 100 per cent and 140 per cent in salaries and allowances. It proposed raising the minimum basic salary from Tk 8,250 to Tk 20,000, while increasing the highest basic salary from Tk 78,000 to Tk 160,000.

The commission had said that, while Tk 1.31 trillion is currently spent on approximately 1.4 million government employees and 900,000 pensioners, an additional Tk 1.06 trillion would be required to implement the new pay structure.

However, sources said the Nasimul Ghani committee did not recommend salary increases of more than 100 per cent. The committee had proposed implementing the new pay structure in two stages over two years: basic salaries from 1 July of the current financial year, followed by allowances from 1 July of the next financial year.

According to Ministry of Finance sources, however, the proposal prepared for submission to the Cabinet differs from the earlier recommendation. Basic salaries will indeed be increased from 1 July, but the increases will be implemented in stages.

Finance Minister Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury announced while presenting the national budget in Parliament on 11 June that the new pay structure for government employees would be implemented in phases from 1 July this year.

In his budget speech, he said government employees had been receiving salaries and allowances under the same pay structure for nearly 11 years. During that period, the cost of living had risen substantially because of inflation. The new pay structure would therefore be implemented in phases from 1 July, he said.

The budget for the current financial year has allocated Tk 141,434 crore for salaries and allowances—Tk 54,572 crore more than the revised allocation for the previous financial year.

Asked where the funding for the new pay structure would come from, Finance Minister Amir Khosru Mahmud Chowdhury told Prothom Alo last week, “We cannot afford to provide it all at once.”

Asked whether even a two-stage implementation would require a substantial amount of money, the finance minister said, “We are working on it. The calculations are under way. The fiscal space has narrowed considerably because of the huge volume of imports. Even if we want to, we cannot afford to provide it all at once.”

item.title: Power crisis disrupts healthcare across the country
item.description:
Fifty-eight-day-old Hafsa Jahan is struggling to breathe. She was admitted to Matlab South Upazila Health Complex in Chandpur last Saturday after developing pneumonia. She is supposed to receive nebuliser treatment several times a day to ease her breathing.

But because there was no electricity at the hospital, she could not receive the treatment properly. The ceiling fan above her bed was also not working. The heat was making her breathing difficulties worse. Her mother, Kamrun Nahar, was holding her sick daughter and waiting for the electricity to return. This was the situation on Sunday.

Like Hafsa's mother, mothers and children in different parts of the country, including Patiya in Chattogram and Raipur in Lakshmipur, are also having to wait for electricity.

Mofassir, a one-and-a-half-year-old pneumonia patient in Patiya, is supposed to receive nebuliser treatment six times a day. But he received it only three times last Saturday. In Raipur, four-year-old Minu Akter, who has pneumonia, needs nebulisation four times a day, but the treatment cannot be provided regularly because of power outages.

Other healthcare services are also being disrupted at upazila-level hospitals.

When electricity goes out, nebulisers, X-ray machines and ECG services stop at some hospitals. Pathology tests are also suspended. In some hospitals, power cuts during surgery have forced staff to switch on generators. In other hospitals, generators are available but there is no fuel.

As a result, patients and their relatives who come to hospitals for treatment have to wait for the electricity to return. During power outages, patients and their attendants also have to endure extreme heat.

These conditions were found during visits to one district hospital and 13 upazila health complexes across the country on Saturday and Sunday, and through conversations with patients, relatives, physicians and healthcare workers.

Alongside a gas shortage, Bangladesh has been facing an electricity shortage for more than a month. Load-shedding decreases occasionally when it rains and increases when temperatures rise. Initially, the power cuts were entirely outside Dhaka. Since the night of 12 August, load-shedding has also been enforced in Dhaka following government instructions. Although the plan was to impose one hour of load-shedding once a day in an area of Dhaka, the schedule is not being followed.

According to data from the Bangladesh Power Development Board (PDB) and Power Grid PLC (PGCB), electricity generation is falling short of demand because of fuel shortages. The effects have now reached upazila-level hospitals.

Surgeries also disrupted

A caesarean section was being performed at Bagmara Upazila Health Complex in Rajshahi about a week ago. The power went out shortly after the surgery began. The sudden darkness caused panic among the patient and her relatives. Eventually, staff used mobile phone lights and quickly bought fuel to start the generator and complete the surgery.

The 50-bed hospital treats a large number of outpatients every day. A visit to the facility on Sunday found that X-ray, laboratory and ECG services were also being disrupted because of load-shedding.

Shankar Kumar Biswas, health and family planning officer at Bagmara Upazila Health Complex, said all hospital activities, including diagnostic tests, come to a standstill when there is no electricity.

Power sometimes goes out even after surgery has begun, creating serious risks. Although one generator has been repaired, it cannot be kept running regularly because there is no allocation for the necessary fuel.

Power outages are also occurring during surgeries at Nilphamari General Hospital.

During a visit to different departments of the hospital on Saturday morning, it was found that power disruptions were causing difficulties with diagnostic tests, surgeries and patient admissions.

Around 1:00pm, relatives of patients crowded outside the operating theatre. A woman named Shapla Begum was taken into the operation theatre for a caesarean section.

About 15 minutes after the surgery began, the electricity went out. Shapla gave birth to a baby girl at that point. The baby was taken out of the operating theatre, but the mother's surgery had not yet been completed and she was still being stitched. The generator was started after a short while and the remaining procedure was completed.

Senior staff nurse Brishti Roy, who is responsible for the operating theatre, said four to five caesarean sections were performed there every day. But because of the power crisis, they can now perform no more than one or two.

"One was performed today (Saturday)," she said.

She said the hospital normally performs five to six surgeries of different types every day, including orthopaedic, ear, nose and throat (ENT) and general surgery. The number of surgeries has fallen because of load-shedding.

Bidhan Chandra Roy, in-charge of the operating theatre, said surgery requires a suitable environment. When the electricity goes out during an operation, the generator has to be switched on. The air conditioner cannot be operated in that situation. If a physician or nurse on duty sweats in such conditions and sweat falls onto the surgical wound, there is a risk of infection.

Generators available, but no fuel

Hospitals are supposed to have generators as an alternative source of power during outages. But several hospitals have generators without fuel.

The only generator at Matlab South Upazila Health Complex in Chandpur is out of service because of a lack of fuel. It requires 15 to 20 litres of fuel a day to operate, but there is no budget allocation to purchase it.

Rajib Kishore Banik, resident medical officer at Matlab South Upazila Health Complex, said the hospital had been experiencing long power outages for several days, with frequent load-shedding.

X-ray, ECG and nebulisation services were being disrupted, he said. The overall delivery of healthcare at the hospital was being affected by the electricity shortage.

Raipur Upazila Health Complex in Lakshmipur also has a generator, but it cannot be operated when needed because there is no allocation for diesel.

Some hospitals do not have generators at all.

At Bera Upazila Health Complex in Pabna, for example, patients and their relatives suffer when the electricity goes out because the hospital has no generator.

Golam Sarwar, in-charge of the pathology department, said diagnostic tests have to be suspended during power outages, leaving patients waiting.

At Kulaura Upazila Health Complex in Moulvibazar, candles have to be lit when the electricity goes out at night. Physicians examine patients in the wards using the flashlights on their mobile phones.

Juri Upazila Health Complex has an IPS backup system provided by a private organisation. It can power one light bulb in each of two wards at night.

Patients forced to go elsewhere for X-rays

Diagnostic services are facing the most direct impact of power disruptions.

At Sakhipur Upazila Health Complex in Tangail, the X-ray machine sometimes stops working because of both load-shedding and low voltage.

During a visit to the hospital on Saturday, Rafiqul Islam from Gargobindapur village was found seeking treatment after being injured in a motorcycle accident. But because the X-ray machine was not functioning, he had to go to a private clinic and pay Tk 500 for the test.

The same test would have cost Tk 55 at the government hospital.

SM Amirul Islam Momen, a medical technologist in the X-ray department at Sakhipur Upazila Health Complex, said the X-ray machine sometimes stops functioning because of low voltage as well as load-shedding.

Kamrul Islam went to Raipur Upazila Health Complex in Lakshmipur on Sunday for an X-ray after fracturing a finger. He waited for about an hour, but the electricity did not return, so he left without undergoing the test.

"I came to the hospital from Charbangshi in Raipur to have an X-ray. I waited for an hour. There is no certainty about when the electricity will return. So I am being forced to leave," he said.

At Manikchhari Upazila Health Complex in Khagrachhari, most X-ray services remain suspended because of low voltage, a visit on Sunday found. Patients are being advised by physicians to go to private clinics and diagnostic centres.

Abdul Wadud, a resident of Matlab South Upazila headquarters, waited for two hours on Sunday after bringing his elderly mother to the health complex for an X-ray. He eventually decided to take her to a nearby private hospital.

Relatives use hand fans beside patients

Load-shedding is not only shutting down equipment. It is also making life difficult for patients admitted to hospitals.

At Bera Upazila Health Complex in Pabna on Sunday, 18-year-old Ashik Hossain was suffering from fever while his mother, Asma Khatun, sat beside him continuously fanning him with a hand fan.

She said the electricity had gone out repeatedly at night. The heat had made her son and other patients restless.

Aleya Khatun, whose 70-year-old husband Amzad Hossain was suffering from diarrhoea, said the repeated power cuts at night had caused her husband considerable discomfort and prevented her from sleeping properly.

At Taraganj Upazila Health Complex in Rangpur, electricity was unavailable for a total of four hours and 45 minutes in five separate outages during the 12-hour period from 7:30am on Saturday.

During a visit to the hospital on Saturday, Shamina Begum, who was suffering from breathing difficulties, said she had been admitted for three days. Her breathing became more difficult whenever the electricity went out.

The nebuliser could not be operated, she said, forcing her to use a hand fan. The electricity sometimes remained off for one and a half to two hours.

Prolonged load-shedding

Patients and relatives at Kulaura and Juri health complexes in Moulvibazar said electricity was unavailable for eight to 12 hours a day, including at night.

At Kulaura Health Complex on Saturday, patient attendant Popy Rani said she had been staying at the hospital for four days with her two-year-old child, who had pneumonia. When the electricity went out at night, they had to use candles.

Load-shedding has increased over the past two to three months in six upazilas of Lakshmipur.

Shafiul Alam, general manager of Lakshmipur Palli Bidyut Samity, said the area was receiving 30 to 35 per cent less electricity than demand.

At Bera in Pabna, according to the local Rural Electrification Board, electricity demand is around 9 megawatts during the day and 12 to 13 megawatts at night.

Against this demand, there is a shortfall of 25 to 30 per cent during the day and 35 to 40 per cent at night, said Uttam Kumar Saha, deputy general manager of the Bera zonal office of Pabna Palli Bidyut Samity-2.

Gas shortage reduces power generation

According to data from the Bangladesh Power Development Board (PDB) and Power Grid PLC (PGCB), electricity generation is falling short of demand because of fuel shortages. As a result, load-shedding has not eased even during the weekly weekend break.

The highest load-shedding on Saturday was recorded at 3:00pm, at 3,612 megawatts. The previous day, Friday, the highest load-shedding was recorded at midnight, at 3,244 megawatts.

The Rural Electrification Board (REB), the country's largest electricity distribution agency, said its highest load-shedding on Friday was 2,673 megawatts. At that time, the electricity deficit in the Mymensingh region stood at 46 per cent.

BB’s net profit reaches Tk26,000cr
item.description:
Bangladesh Bank has earned a massive profit in the recently concluded FY26.
Over the past year, the central bank recorded a net profit of Tk25,977 crore.
This profit was largely driven by weak banks borrowing from Bangladesh Bank at higher interest rates to meet their daily operational needs.
The earnings mark an increase of Tk3,357 crore compared to the previous fiscal year.
The final financial statement for the last fiscal year was approved today, Sunday, at a board of directors meeting held in the Bangladesh Bank conference room, chaired by Governor Mostakur Rahman.
With the consent of the board members, a performance bonus equivalent to six basic salaries was approved for Bangladesh Bank officials and employees.
The central bank deposits its entire profit into the government treasury.
The government has already received Tk10,000 crore, while the remaining Tk15,977 crore will be deposited into the government's account shortly, helping meet its development expenditure needs.
According to Bangladesh Bank data, the organization’s net profit in FY25 stood at Tk22,620 crore, reflecting significant growth in FY26.
Prior to that, in FY24, the central bank made a gross profit of nearly Tk40,000 crore, with a net profit of Tk15,300 crore.
Despite an economic slowdown, the central bank’s credit management activities remained brisk during the last fiscal year.
Due to a liquidity crunch, many commercial banks borrowed funds from Bangladesh Bank at higher interest rates to cover daily requirements.
The central bank earned substantial interest income on these loans.
Additionally, Bangladesh Bank’s foreign exchange reserves are invested in international bonds and various countries; due to rising global interest rates, these investments also yielded significant returns.
However, banking insiders point out that generating profit is not the central bank’s primary objective.
As a regulatory body, its core duties involve supervising the banking sector, controlling inflation, boosting private sector investment, and generating employment.
According to experts, the surge in Bangladesh Bank's profit stems mainly from instability in the economy and the banking sector.
They caution that in the pursuit of profit, the central bank must ensure it does not stray from its primary objective of maintaining money market stability.

item.title: Elections loom, yet administrators being installed in Union Parishads
item.description:
• Number of Union Parishads in the country: 4,588.

  • Number of eligible unions for election: 311.

  • Elections cannot be held in 4,237 unions as their tenures have not expired. Cases are ongoing in 40 unions.

The government is planning to start holding Union Parishad (UP) elections within this year, and the election commission (EC) is preparing accordingly, with the schedule likely to be announced in September. However, the government is currently appointing administrators to the Union Parishads.

According to Ministry of Local Government sources, administrators have been appointed to at least 38 Union Parishads over the past two months. Among these, 31 are old unions and seven are newly formed.

In some places, government officials have been appointed as administrators, while in others, leaders of the ruling BNP (Bangladesh Nationalist Party) have been placed in these posts. Party leaders have also been appointed as Union Parishad members.

Sources in the Ministry of Local Government indicated that the process of appointing administrators to more Union Parishads is currently underway.

The Ministry of Local Government reasons that the government made this decision to keep public services running smoothly. There is no legal bar to appointing administrators under the law.

State Minister for Local Government Mir Shahe Alam told newspersons at the Secretariat on 17 July that elections to five tiers of local government will be held within this year.

When asked by Prothom Alo why administrators were being appointed under such circumstances, he said the appointments have no relation to the elections and the Union Parishad elections will indeed be held within this year.

When asked why party affiliates are being appointed as administrators to Union Parishads, the state minister said the list of administrators is sent to the ministry from the deputy commissioner's office. It only contains individual names, so there is no opportunity to know who is a government official or a political party leader.

The number of Union Parishads in the country is 4,588. According to data from the Ministry of Local Government, as of 30 July, the number of election-eligible unions was 311. Elections cannot be held in 4,237 unions as their tenures have not expired, and lawsuits are ongoing in 40.

Following the fall of the Awami League government in the July mass uprising on 5 August 2024, many Union Parishad chairmen went into hiding. During the tenure of the interim government, administrators were appointed from among government officials in many places. However, no party affiliates were appointed at that time.

The BNP government has now appointed party affiliates as administrators in several Union Parishads. Sources say local BNP leaders are trying to place party affiliates as administrators in more unions.

Earlier in July, the government made one-year contractual appointments of BNP leaders to top posts in 11 government institutions. BNP leaders have also been appointed as administrators in 11 city corporations, 63 district councils and 8 urban development authorities.

Party leaders as UP administrators

According to sources in the Ministry of Local Government, Faruque Hossain Khokon was given the responsibility of administrator in Mokamia Union of Betagi upazila in Barguna last month. He is the joint convener of Betagi Upazila BNP.

In the Baushia Union Parishad of Gazaria upazila in Munshiganj, Ebadul Haque was appointed as the new administrator. He was the former joint secretary of the upazila Jubo Dal and the member for Ward No. 3 of Baushia Union, where he had previously served as a member.

In Rupganj Union Parishad of Narayanganj, BNP leader Md. Noor Nabi Bhuiyan was appointed as administrator on 19 July. Concurrently, the Local Government Division appointed 12 BNP leaders and activists of various levels as members of the council.

Fazlur Rahman Bhuiyan was appointed as the administrator of Barishal Union Parishad in Akhaura upazila of Brahmanbaria. He is a member of the Brahmanbaria district unit BNP.

Comprising both newly formed and old unions, out of the 38 Union Parishads where administrators were appointed in the past two months, 19 are in Barishal district, representing the highest number.

Sources said that after the tenures of the Union Parishads in Bakerganj, Muladi, and Wazirpur upazilas of Barishal ended, multiple meetings were held regarding appointing BNP leaders as administrators. However, no consensus was reached on who would be selected.

Abul Hossain Khan, Member of Parliament for the Barishal-6 Bakerganj constituency, told Prothom Alo that many leaders want to become Union Parishad administrators.

"If we give it to one, another gets unhappy, which is why no one was appointed. To avoid controversy, administrators are being appointed from among government officials," he said.

The Local Government (Union Parishad) Act states that an administrator will be appointed for a single term of 120 days, though the government can extend the term. If the government wishes, it can run the Union Parishads through administrators without holding elections.

Badiul Alam Majumdar, Secretary of Shushashoner Jonno Nagorik (SHUJAN) told Prothom Alo that if elections are held soon, there is no need to appoint administrators for a short period.

"It is necessary to stop appointing party affiliates to government posts. The government should hold elections as soon as possible. If administrators are appointed instead of holding elections, many may begin to suspect that elections might not be held in all unions," he said.

1,000 Rohingya to receive skills training under China-backed program
item.description:
A skills development program for 1,000 Rohingya has been launched at Camp 11 in Ukhiya, Cox’s Bazar, with support from the Embassy of the People’s Republic of China in Bangladesh.
National humanitarian development organization Impact Initiative inaugurated the program, titled “Sustainable Opportunities for Livelihoods, Advancement and Resilience (SOLAR),” at the Multipurpose Building of Rohingya Camp 11 on Tuesday.
Md Shariful Islam, deputy secretary and Camp-in-Charge of Camp 11, attended the inauguration as the chief guest, while Impact Initiative Chief Executive Officer Md Enayet Hossain chaired the event.
Under the SOLAR initiative, 325 participants will receive practical, market-oriented technical training in tailoring and dressmaking, block printing and batik, mobile phone servicing, gas burner repair and climate-smart agriculture.
Another 675 participants will receive soft-skills training focused on communication, teamwork, problem-solving, workplace behavior and other essential life and employability skills.
Speaking at the inauguration, Shariful Islam said skills development and practical livelihood training could play an important role in strengthening the capacity and self-reliance of the Rohingya community.
“Initiatives such as SOLAR will help participants develop practical skills and prepare themselves for future livelihood opportunities,” he said.
Enayet Hossain said Impact Initiative was creating opportunities for the Rohingya community to develop practical and market-relevant skills with support from the Chinese Embassy.
“Through the SOLAR initiative, we aim to strengthen their capacity, resilience and prospects for sustainable livelihoods,” he said.
The initiative aims to complement humanitarian assistance with skills development and livelihood-focused interventions, helping Rohingya community members build practical capacities and improve their prospects for self-reliance amid prolonged displacement.
With support from the Chinese Embassy and implementation by Impact Initiative, the program is expected to expand skills and livelihood opportunities for Rohingya community members in the camp.

Day 1 of the two-day international conference, ‘Act For Nutrition: The Emergency We Can No Longer Ignore’ — held at Islamabad’s Serena Hotel — concluded on Wednesday, with experts urging urgent action on Pakistan’s malnutrition and stunting crisis, with a focus on multisectoral interventions.

With more than 40 per cent of children under five stunted, a maternal mortality rate of 155 deaths per 100,000 live births, and malnutrition costing Pakistan upwards of $17 billion annually, the country stands at a crossroads: continue on the current trajectory and surrender an entire generation’s potential, or choose a different future.

The two-day conference is bringing together policymakers, international development leaders, health professionals and nutrition experts to confront the burgeoning crisis and build momentum for urgent, coordinated action.

The focus of discussions will be on moving the national conversation beyond statistics towards practical, measurable interventions that can improve nutrition outcomes and protect Pakis­tan’s human capital and future generations.

View the full agenda here.

5:27pm - Day 1 of the conference concludes

5:15pm - Researcher calls for nutrition-related interventions at community, systemic levels

Director at the International Research Force Dr Hana Mahmood said focus on nutrition was needed at the community, systemic, and legislative levels.

Remarking on awareness campaigns on the community level, she said, “Interventions are not designed according to the latest theories and latest approaches towards designing behaviour change”.

She stressed a multisectoral approach to nutrition, adding that “no specific industry owns nutrition”.

5:00pm - Doctor stresses rigorous testing for pregnant women

Dr Nosheen Ashraf of the National Institutes of Health, speaking about maternal nutrition, said that during antenatal visits, mothers are asked to take supplements to address nutritional deficiencies; however, she noted a lack of consistent monitoring.

Dr Ashraf said there were not enough laboratories in far-flung areas, as she called for rigorous testing of pregnant mothers to track any nutritional deficiencies.

4:55pm - Gynaecologist stresses nutrition should not be limited to pregnancy or childbirth

Capital Hospital Associate Gynaecologist Dr Urooj Yasir Khan said the focus of nutrition should not be limited to pregnancy or childbirth.

“There is hardly any awareness about nutrition in our adolescent girl groups.” Following a substantial loss of iron during menstruation, micronutrient deficiencies in the body at the onset of pregnancy, especially if it’s a teenage pregnancy, can lead to growth-restricted babies, she said.

Commenting on treatment for obesity, she said, “we don’t say what’s important to eat”, adding that the focus seems to be on the number of calories consumed.

4:53pm - Founder Nutradevice calls for equitable access to nutritious food

Founder Nutradevice Dr Nosheen Taqvi held that creating awareness about nutritious food did not guarantee nutrition; rather, she maintained that it was worth examining “if the mother can access it, implement it, afford it and keeping in view the power of the woman in the household, can she give it to the children”.

Dr Taqvi also clarified misconceptions around nutrition. “It is not true that healthy food is always expensive [..] as you don’t always have to focus on animal-based food”.

She also noted that mothers in Pakistani households did not prioritise themselves. “Food is given to the family first. and then the mother eats whatever is left of it.”

She also noted that stigma around weight gain was leading to nutritional deficiencies in women as well.

4:38pm - Researcher explains why ‘1,000-day’ period is critical to addressing malnutrition

Director of the International Research Force Dr Hana Mahmood explained why the first 1,000-day period of an infant’s life remained critical in addressing malnutrition.

“The most important thing we have to attend to right now is that these 1,000 days are those days in which growth is exponentially high and the requirement for micronutrients is massive,” Dr Mahmood said.

She added that during this time, the immune system and major organs were developing in such a way that any lack in nutritional input could lead to irreversible damage.

“During the first two years of life, 80pc of a child’s brain develops,” she said. Dr Mahmood also noted that Pakistan had one of the highest child-under-five mortality rates, a majority of which was contributed by malnutrition.

“250m deaths can be averted by focusing on prevention of stunting,” she said.

4:27pm - Session titled ‘First 1,000 days: Why women and girls matter for nutrition’ begins

4:10pm - Agri consultant highlights need for demand pull in producing nutritionally rich food

Agriculture consultant Hasan Khurrum Hanif, talking about producing nutritionally dense food, said, “Pakistani farmers need a demand pull, rather than a supply push”.

“Farmers will produce what you pay us to produce and if there is a market where I can sell zinc-fortified wheat, where I can sell vegetables with lower pesticide residue, all of those require a different input package, which has a cost component,” he said.

Hanif added that processors needed to provide farmers an ecosystem.

3:55pm - Food safety infrastructure critical for nutrition, economy, says Tetra Pak executive

Corporate Affairs Director at Tetra Pak Noor Aftab stressed the significance of food safety, saying that “food systems need to be treated as critical infrastructure”.

He said that Pakistan is one of the largest milk-producing countries, but there were no safe milk or pasteurisation laws in the country, depriving the economy of $30bn export potential.

He added that in Pakistan, milk is taxed at one of the highest rates in the world. “If there is a resilient food systems infrastructure built within Pakistan, coupled with sustainable fiscal roadmaps… that will allow […] the infrastructure to act as a catalyst for nourishment and improvement.”

3:45pm - Nutrition investment reduced absenteeism rate in Bangladesh, says official

Project Manager at the Workforce Nutrition GM Reza Sumon, joining the conference through video conference from Bangladesh, discussed nutrition investments for the workforce.

He said that in Bangladesh’s government sector, the anaemia rate within the workforce was at 51.9pc. However, after interventions via funding for fortified rice, oils and iron and folic acid tablets, the anaemia rate dropped to 32pc, Sumon said, which helped convince the private sector to make similar investments in nutrition.

He said after the private sector invested $10m in nutrition in the past year, absenteeism in workplaces has reduced from 70pc to 40pc.

3:40pm - EBM executive shares details on a fortified biscuits initiative

Head of Corporate Communications & Sustainability at English Biscuit Manufacturers (EBM) Attiyah Inaam Khan shared details of an initiative launched by the company in which fortified biscuits were provided to mothers to address malnutrition.

“We tracked them for five years, and mothers who received biscuits showed great iron levels during pregnancy, and children born under the study showed stronger cognitive development,” she recalled.

“It is not about margins but more about whether there is evidence on the ground and whether the intervention can be scalable,” she added.

“Government can also play a very important lever here: tax credit for fortification in products and reduce the import duty on fortification,” she added.

3:36pm - Session on mobilising private capital and partnerships begins

A panel discussion on mobilising private capital and partnerships has begun.

3:12pm - ADB views malnutrition as an economic issue, working with BISP, says official

Senior Project Officer at Asian Development Bank (ADB) Mansoor Ali Masood said the bank was looking at malnutrition through an economic lens rather than viewing it solely as a health issue.

“Hence, we are trying to mainstream it through social protection, education, agriculture and water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) services,” he said, adding that ADB was supporting the Benazir Nashonuma Programme and had allocated around half of a $960m fund to address stunting.

“ADB is supporting the expansion of BNP, helping BISP in expanding the awareness of mothers who are better informed and can take better decisions for their children and ensure dietary diversity.”

3:07pm - ‘Nutrition is part of human capital’

The Dean of Research at Pakistan Institute of Development Economics (PIDE) Dr Shujaat Farooq, said that the economic cost of malnutrition was “too much”.

Citing statistics, he said 40pc of children in the country are facing stunting while 25 million children are out of school. He added that 75pc of children in schools were unable to learn proficiently due to malnutrition.

“Nutrition is part of human capital,” Farooq said.

3:00pm - No multi-sectoral nutrition programmes in the past decade: Planning ministry official

Chief of nutrition at the planning ministry, Dr Nazeer Ahmed, said in the past “one to two decades, there had been no major nutrition programme implemented in the provinces, except the Benazir Nashonuma Programme”.

“We have the policies in the four provinces, and nutrition strategies [..] But on the ground, we do not have any multi-sectoral programmes implemented,” he said.

2:55pm - Nutrition not often framed as GDP statistic: Gates Foundation official

Gates Foundation Senior Programme Officer of Development Policy and Finance Dr Ammar Malik said that according to World Bank statistics, for every dollar a government invested in nutrition, it could get up to $23 back in the form of economic benefits.

Questioning why such a high return on investment was still ignored, Malik said one of the issues was that nutrition investments were long-term, with returns becoming obvious years or decades later.

He added another issue was that nutrition is seen as a standalone topic in such discussions, instead of framing it as a gross domestic product statistic.

“If I were to say to you that Pakistan is losing 3pc of its GDP because of lack of investment in nutrition, that is a much stronger argument for economic policymakers than it is to talk about nutrition,” he said.

2:50pm - Gates Foundation official says Pakistan’s crisis is a ‘balance sheet problem’

Gates Foundation’s Dr Ammar Malik, who serves as the senior programme officer of development policy and finance, said the nutrition problem in Pakistan was a “balance sheet problem”.

“The government of Pakistan can either now decide to spend more on nutrition today through our budgets, or we can pay the price of this lack of investment in the form of lost gross domestic product over the next several years or even decades,” he said.

2:45pm — ‘Nutrition has few dedicated champions’

Global Alliance for Improved Nutrition Executive Director Lawrence Haddad noted that another reason nutrition was underfunded was a lack of dedicated efforts towards the issue.

“Why is this? Well, because malnutrition is multi-sectoral. It is the interaction of poor diet, poor water, poor sanitation, poor healthcare, and poor care in general, and so each of these areas has its own ministry.”

“There is no ministry of nutrition,” he added.

2:42pm — Expert says malnutrition underfunded despite ‘catastrophic consequences’

The session on investing in nutrition began with a video note by Global Alliance for Improved Nutrition Executive Director Lawrence Haddad, who pointed out that malnutrition remained underfunded “despite its catastrophic impact”.

“Forty five per cent of children’s deaths under three worldwide are due to malnutrition,” Haddad noted, adding that less than 1pc of international aid was spent on malnutrition.

“It is quite invisible in many ways,” he added.

2:30pm — Conference resumes after lunch break

1:50pm - Lunch break

The conference will resume at 2:30pm.

1:40pm- WHO official says ‘no bigger risk than lack of action’

Ellen Thom, the deputy representative for the World Health Organisation Pakistan warned that “there was no bigger risk than the lack of action” in addressing malnutrition.

“As we speak, before I finish answering, [..] in the next three minutes, at least 14 children will have died across the world from causes related to maternal and child malnutrition,” Thom said, adding that such deaths were preventable and “we cannot afford not to take action”.

She also noted that Pakistan was suffering an annual economic loss of $17bn due to stunting and malnutrition.

1:34pm - WFP official says malnutrition not just driven by poverty

Thomas Conan, the deputy country director for the World Food Programme, said that malnutrition was not just driven by poverty.

“It is also directly influenced and fed by poor access to services … health services and water and sanitation services,” he said.

1:15pm - Expert calls for focusing on adolescent nutrition

Food security adviser on nutrition and social protection at GIZ Pakistan, Dr Faiza Wahab, raised the alarm at the “missing adolescent middle” during conversations about malnutrition.

She said that nutrition discourse had been focused on the first 1,000 days of a child, but she stressed, “we are really missing the middle, which is between childhood and motherhood”.

“Focusing on adolescent nutrition is not to prepare them for motherhood, but it is also a window where the investment really returns in the form of human capital development,” she said.

She explained that during adolescent years, young girls were vulnerable to anaemia and iron deficiencies due to “rapid growth, hormonal changes and menstruation”.

“If she is not empowered, she cannot participate in education, and she has less cognitive capabilities,” Dr Wahab said.

1:10pm - WHO official stresses need for integrating social protection programmes with health services

Ellen Thom, the deputy representative for the World Health Organisation Pakistan, said integrating social protection with existing health and nutrition services is important.

She said that evidence showed that doing so and strengthening integrated primary healthcare was an effective way of reaching vulnerable families and delivering high-impact nutrition interventions.

1:02pm - WFP official says nutrition is not just about food

Thomas Conan, the deputy country director for the World Food Programme, said that nutrition was not only about food.

“It’s not only about access to food. It is about a healthy diet, the capacity to ensure multi-sectoral intervention and collaboration among us,” he said.

He said that it was also necessary to ensure access to a more healthy diet and the design of the social protection was nutrition-sensitive,” he said.

12:50pm - BISP official talks about Nashonuma programme

BISP Director General Dr Asim Ijaz spoke about the Benazir Nashonuma Programme (BNP), which he said had added a “nutritional and health layer” to the existing BISP registry.

He stressed that there exists a 1,000-day window for a child’s development, during which “irreversible damage can occur”.

“This is why BISP changed its thinking in 2019,” he said. He said that the recognition was then realised in the Nashonuma pilot launch in 2020, which was then phased out country-wide in 2021.

“Nashonuma itself is not a separate bureaucracy but layered onto existing platforms,” he said, explaining that BISP’s registry was now carrying a nutritional and health layer.

“So the idea was to have one beneficiary record with multiple beneficial layers,” he said.

12:42pm - ‘We can no longer afford to look away,’ BISP chairperson says

Senator Rubina Khalid, the chairperson of Benazir Income Support Programme, said in her keynote address that the responsibility lay not just with providing financial assistance, but with also helping families move from vulnerability towards dignity.

“We have gathered here today … because we can no longer afford to look away,” she said. She said that more than 40pc of children under five in Pakistan were stunted, while malnutrition placed a huge burden on the economy.

“Stunting is not only a health issue. It is a human capital issue, an economic issue and a challenge to Pakistan’s future,” she said. She said that the country lacked integration of the programmes it had to address these issues.

At the end of her address, she said: “We must work together so that every child in Pakistan has the opportunity to grow, learn and reach their full potential. Because every child we protect from malnutrition is not simply a life protected, it is the future protected, a family strengthened and a stronger Pakistan secured.”

12:40pm: Session on integrating nutrition into social protection systems begins

A session on integrating nutrition into social protection systems begins.

12:30pm - Sri Lankan doctor calls for understanding child growth trajectory in South Asia

Dr Rannan-Eliya, in answer to a question, pointed out that the child growth trajectory in South Asia was not the same as the rest of the world.

“We have sort of misunderstood the problem,” he remarked, adding: “There is no uniformity in child growth, and because we use a single growth standard, we partly misdiagnose what is going on”.

“In my sense, Sri Lankan kids need to be better nourished but there is a limit to what we can do and we need to understand that,” he said. He noted that a similar understanding was also being realised in India.

“So we need to do more as South and South East Asian countries, and it’s something that needs better investigation, and it is leading to a misunderstanding of what the problem is.”

12:13pm - Expert says nutrition an issue of human capital, economic growth

Dr Irshad Danish, the co-chair of the Global Nutrition Report Stakeholder Group, said that from his experience, Pakistan had low allocation, fragmented spending and implementation challenges.

“If we need $10 to feed malnourished children, we are spending only $2,” he said. He added that Pakistan was losing $17bn annually due to malnutrition.

He said that this also resulted in poor education outcomes, children with cognitive issues and lower workforce productivity.

“So, nutrition is not just a health issue. It is an issue of human capital and economic growth,” he said. He said that the cost of malnutrition was far greater than the cost of prevention.

“We need to move from fragmented spending towards strategic investment, and from hidden allocations to transparent budgets,” he said.

12:00pm - Doctor stresses importance of lady health workers

Co-chair of the Global Nutrition Report Stakeholder Group Dr Irshad Danish stressed the significance of the lady health workers programme.

“It was one of the strongest community based health workers model and its coverage was around 60pc, with over 100,000 lady health workers,” he said, adding that the workers enjoyed community ownership.

“These workers were often the first link of access for healthcare [..] many independent evaluation where these health workers were available, there was better health knowledge and better access to essential services.”

11:46am - Sri Lankan official explains how country scaled health systems

Dr Ravi Rannan-Eliya, the executive director of Sri Lanka’s Institute of Health Policy, said that 100 years ago, the South Asian country had worse health outcomes than the rest of the region.

“We were the sick man of South Asia, but now we have the best health plan. How did that happen? One simple reason I always tell people was the ballot box … the British decided to give self-rule,” he said.

He said that as a consequence, there was a pressure to give free education and to expand health services. He said that voters prioritised access to care over all other things.

11:42am - Session on South and South-East Asia’s current realities

The session on South and South-East Asia’s current realities has now begun.

11:30am- Scaling Up Nutrition movement official highlights its progress

Asia Regional Representative of the Scaling Up Nutrition (SUN) Movement Dr Srikanth Eadara spoke about the objectives of the movement, which he said was comprised of 67 countries and was a country-led global nutrition advocacy platform.

“It unites different stakeholders coming from civil society, private sector, donors, UN, agencies and other entities as well as youth to end malnutrition,” he said, adding that it was launched in 2013 to “ ensure a coordinated multisectoral and multi-stakeholder action to address malnutrition in all its forms”.

“We are currently in the fourth phase of the SUN Movement, and it is based on the current challenges and current context of nutrition, which shows that, yes, there is progress; however, the progress is slow and uneven,” he noted.

Dr Eadara also spoke of the issues surrounding nutrition finance, highlighting that the cost of malnutrition was “estimated to be around 5 to 11pc of the total GDPs of Asia and Africa”.

He warned that recent funding cuts, particularly in the World Health Organisation have “threatened to reverse progress” made on nutrition.

“The reduction will also result in increased hardships and deaths, with a lot of implications for public health and economic growth and stability,” he said.

11:25am - Doctor says nutrition the ‘outcome of many systems’

Dr Aminah Jahangir, the global lead for health and nutrition at the Aga Khan Foundation, said that nutrition is the outcome of many systems and cannot be solved by one. She said that climate was already shaping the conditions in which children grow.

“Our experience suggests that the outcomes are better where health services, food systems and community institutions have worked around the same household over many years. It reminds us that progress is achievable in our own context,” she said.

11:20am - Social protection can address malnutrition, says WFP official

The WFP official spoke of one of the three priorities the organisation held for its work in South Asia was advocacy for policy engagement.

She explained, “this is a continuous effort to work with governments from South Asia to highlight how social protection can be more than a safety net and more than a poverty reduction instrument”.

Hobbs said that with the right intentions, social protection held promise to improve nutrition, diets and address malnutrition.

“This is because social protection already reaches the families that are the most vulnerable and those are the families that face the highest challenges,” she added.

11:12am: WFP official says over 80pc of stunted children come from middle-income countries

Asia Pacific Regional Nutrition Adviser for the World Food Programme Nora Hobbs, in her address, spoke of the geographical realities of stunting, stating that the majority of children affected by stunting are from middle-income countries.

“Over 80pc of the world’s stunted children are in middle-income countries,” she said.

The WFP official continued: “This means that low-income countries may have the highest rate and prevalence, but because middle-income countries have such a large population, it may have higher numbers of stunted children.”

She stressed that the facts highlighted that stunting was a result of “inequalities within countries”.

11:05am - Expert highlights need for coordinated response

Dr Giacomo Zanello, an associate professor of Food Economics and Health at the University of Reading, said that neither food nor the health systems could solve malnutrition alone.

“Progress requires coordinated action across food systems, health systems and social protection. Countries that built integrated approaches before crisis struck, were able to keep essential services running through disruption,” he said.

“Integration cannot be improvised during a crisis. It has to be done in advance,” he said.

11:00am - Expert says 2.6bn people cannot afford a healthy diet

Dr Giacomo Zanello, an associate professor of Food Economics and Health at the University of Reading, presented a report on global nutrition.

“Around the world, progress on nutrition is under increasing pressure. Climate shocks, conflict, economic uncertainty … are affecting food and health systems,” he said.

He said that the 2026 global nutrition report focused on how countries can build healthy diets, through stronger integration of food and health systems while building resilience.

“Today, 2.6 billion cannot afford a healthy diet,” he said. He said that extreme weather, rising food prices and pressure on health services were arriving alongside conflict and instability, which was affecting food and health systems.

10:55am - Session on global and regional realities begins

The session on global and regional realities has now begun.

10:52am - UN official says nutrition should not be activated only after a crisis

Pernille Ironside, the United Nations’ resident coordinator in Pakistan, said that communities must be at the heart of the response to malnutrition and stunting.

“Investing in front line workers and community-based platforms and listening to communities themselves can strengthen the uptake of essential services and practices, reinforce local ownership and ensure that women and children most at risk are reached,” she said.

She said that Pakistan knew better than most how quickly climate disasters, economic shocks and displacement can undermine years of development programmes.

“Nutrition, therefore, cannot be something we activate only after a crisis. It needs to be built into the preparedness, into the anticipatory action and the shock responsive systems so that vulnerable families are identified beforehand,” she said.

10:46am - UN official says malnutrition an ‘emergency we can no longer ignore’

Pernille Ironside, the United Nations’ resident coordinator in Pakistan, said that malnutrition was an “emergency we can no longer ignore”.

“When we talk about nutrition, we are not only talking about what a child eats. We are talking about whether a child reaches their full potential. We are talking about the strength of Pakistan’s capital. Nutrition is not only a health issue, it’s a development issue, an economic issue and an issue of equity and opportunity,” she said.

She said that children living in poorer and remote areas were more likely to be left behind. She also said that at the same time, Pakistan faced a growing burden of obesity-related diseases.

10:40am - World Bank official says malnutrition barrier to health, prosperity of individuals, nations

Abigail Perry, the lead nutrition specialist at the World Bank, said malnutrition was a fundamental barrier to the health and prosperity of individuals, communities and nations.

“When a child’s development suffers early in life, the effects can last a lifetime,” she said. She said that the challenge for Pakistan was how to act at the scale, speed and quality required.

10:35am - WHO chief says nutrition is not just about food

World Health Organisation Director General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said nutrition was not only about food.

“It is about access to safe, healthy, diets and strong food systems. Government, academia, civil society and the private sector all have a role to play,” he said.

10:30am - WHO chief says malnutrition one of the greatest barriers to health, development and opportunity

World Health Organisation Director General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, in a recorded message, said that malnutrition remained one of the greatest barriers to health, development and opportunity.

“Every year, it contributes to millions of preventable deaths,” he said. He said that the problem was not a lack of knowledge, rather a lack of action.

10:20am - Minister says equity begins in the womb

Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal said that the Pakistan of 2047 is being built today.

“It is being built in the health of our mothers. It is being built in the nutrition of our infants. It is being built in our homes and communities and it is being built in the developing minds and bodies of our youngest children,” he said.

“We all have to work as a whole,” he said, calling for the conference to spur action.

“Let this be our commitment: every child nourished is protected, every child given a fair start brings Pakistan one step closer to the future we seek,” he said.

10:10am - Minister says investment in nutrition is not charity

“Pakistan cannot win the economic race of the 21st century if millions of children begin the race of life several steps behind than others. There can be no knowledge economy without developing the capacity of the human brain. There can be no productivity revolution without healthy and capable workers. There can be no genuine equality if inequality begins before a child is even born,” said Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal.

“Therefore, investment in nutrition is not charity, it is economic policy,” he said.

10:03am - Minister says first 5 years of a child’s life critical

Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal said that human resource development had not been prioritised in the past. He appreciated the initiative by DawnMedia Group to address the nutrition crisis and called on civil society to take up social issues.

“90 per cent of a children’s brain develops by the age of five .. so the first five years in the life of a child are the most critical,” he said.

“If we fail to develop that human infrastructure during the earliest years of life, we weaken every other investment we subsequently make,” he said.

“That is why stunting cannot remain merely a statistic. For the planning minister, it is a national development challenge,” he said.

9:57am - Planning minister says quality of human resource critical for countries

In his remarks, Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal, the chief guest, conveyed Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s firm commitment to addressing malnutrition and stunting as a national development priority.

He said that as the planning minister, he spent much of his time dealing with the architecture of Pakistan’s development.

“We discuss motorways, energy, dams and digital networks. All of these are essential, but there is one investment more fundamental than all others: the investment in human development,” he said.

“Ultimately it is humans and people who build nations. Therefore, the quality of human resource is critical for any country,” he said.

9:55am - Dawn CEO says nutrition crisis does not ‘look the same’ across the country

Dawn CEO Nazafreen Saigol Lakhani said the nutrition crisis did not “look the same in Tharparkar as it does in Chitral or in southern Punjab”, adding that the response could not be the same either.

“You will hear the economics of financing nutrition, the science of why children fail to grow even when food is technically available, and, I hope, the voices of the women and the mothers who carry the heaviest share of this burden and are so rarely asked to speak about it,” she said.

“With all those who have a role to play gathered around the same table, we have an opportunity to move from recognition of the scale of the problem towards urgent, coordinated and measurable action — action that can improve maternal and child nutrition, strengthen Pakistan’s human capital, and give future generations the opportunity to grow, learn and thrive,” she said.

“That is what this conference ultimately aims to achieve: to build a shared understanding of what needs to be done, and to begin charting a clear and practical roadmap for how we get there,” she added.

9:53am - Dawn CEO says nutrition not a problem for health ministry to solve alone

Dawn CEO Nazafreen Saigol Lakhani said that Pakistan loses close to $17 billion a year to the consequences of malnutrition, “more than what we typically borrow from the International Monetary Fund in any given year”.

“We spend enormous energy negotiating that borrowing. We spend comparatively little energy addressing a loss nearly as large, happening quietly, inside our own households,” she said.

“So this conference starts from a simple premise: nutrition is not a problem for a health ministry to solve alone. It sits at the intersection of health, agriculture, water, education, social protection, our economy and ultimately, our national security,” she added.

She said that countries such as Bangladesh, Peru, and Rwanda had demonstrated that stunting can be dramatically reduced within a generation, but “only when a nation decides, at the highest levels, that the future of its children is important enough to make it a collective priority”.

9:52am - Dawn CEO calls stunting crisis ‘a national emergency’

In her welcome remarks, Dawn CEO Nazafreen Saigol Lakhani said that four out of every ten children under the age of five in Pakistan were stunted.

“These are children whose physical growth and cognitive development may be permanently compromised – often before they have spoken their first words, entered a classroom or had the slightest chance to even dream of their own future,” she said.

“And when this is the reality for four out of every ten children in our country, we cannot merely call it a health problem. It is a national emergency – and a profound failure of our collective priorities,” she said.

9:45am - Conference begins

The conference has begun with the playing of the national anthem and the recitation of the Holy Quran.

item.title: Barclays faces complaint over backing for power plant near world’s largest mangrove forest
item.description:
Bangladeshi complainants allege Rampal power station’s pollution and climate risks threaten the Sunderbans, a world heritage site

Barclays Bank is facing a formal complaint over its financial links to a coal-fired power station near the Sundarbans, the world’s largest mangrove forest and home to millions of people in Bangladesh and India.

Three complainants from the region have submitted a case to the UK government’s Office for Responsible Business Conduct, alleging that the British bank breached international guidelines by underwriting companies involved in the emission-heavy Maitree super thermal power project, also known as the Rampal power plant.
